title: How Thanksgiving became a national holiday: 10 milestones

 How Thanksgiving became a national holiday, traced through 10 milestones from a 1621 Plymouth harvest gathering to Lincoln's 1863 proclamation and Roosevelt's 1939 "Franksgiving" calendar fight
 1 / 12 List slides From Lincoln to "Franksgiving": 10 turning points in the history of the Thanksgiving date List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 2, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 Thanksgiving's place on the fourth Thursday of November comes from federal law, not colonial tradition. Congress put the date into law with a joint resolution, which Franklin D. Roosevelt signed on December 26, 1941. From Lincoln's time until then, the date rested on a proclamation each president issued every autumn. In 1939 that arrangement produced a national argument over which Thursday counted.
 The story of how Thanksgiving became a national holiday runs through religious decrees, wartime politics, a magazine editor's persistence and a retail calendar. Popular memory starts it at Plymouth in 1621, when English colonists and Wampanoag men shared a harvest meal. The colonists themselves did not call that gathering a thanksgiving. In New England, the word meant something else: a solemn day of prayer, often tied to a harvest or a military result.
 National leaders borrowed that religious model. The Continental Congress recommended a thanksgiving day after the victory at Saratoga in 1777. George Washington proclaimed another in 1789. Both were single occasions. As president, Thomas Jefferson declined to issue such proclamations. He held that the federal government had no power to direct religious exercises. For decades, whether the country marked a national thanksgiving in a given year depended on who held office.
 That changed during the Civil War. Sarah Josepha Hale, editor of Godey's Lady's Book, had written to governors and presidents since the 1840s urging one shared date. In 1863 Abraham Lincoln set aside the last Thursday of November for a national thanksgiving. Later presidents repeated the proclamation annually, and the late-November Thursday hardened into custom. Custom was still not law, as Roosevelt showed when he moved the holiday a week earlier.
 The 10 slides that follow trace a selection of turning points in that history rather than every proclamation or local observance. Each one centers on a single moment or decision: what happened, who acted and what it changed. Taken together, they show a holiday that moved from scattered religious observance to annual presidential habit and, finally, to a date written into federal statute. Read in order, they also explain why Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday rather than the last one.
 The 1621 Plymouth harvest feast with the Wampanoag 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 1621 harvest gathering at Plymouth Colony is the event most Americans picture as the start of Thanksgiving. The colonists did not call it a thanksgiving, though. It was a harvest celebration held once, and it did not begin a yearly tradition.
 Most of what is known about the gathering comes from a short letter by Edward Winslow, one of the colony's leaders. The letter was printed in London in 1622 as part of Mourt's Relation, an early account of the Plymouth settlement. In it, Winslow described the colonists celebrating after they brought in their crops.
 Winslow's account names Massasoit, the Wampanoag leader. It says about 90 Wampanoag men joined the English settlers. The colony was small and vulnerable at the time. The Mayflower passengers had arrived in late 1620, and roughly half of them died during the first winter.
 The two groups had political reasons to meet. Massasoit and the Plymouth colonists had agreed to an alliance in the spring of 1621. The pact committed each side to defend the other. The Wampanoag had their own interests in the arrangement, including rivalries with neighboring nations such as the Narragansett.
 Winslow's letter names two kinds of food: fowl and deer. It does not list the dishes found on modern holiday tables. He also mentions recreation, including the colonists exercising their arms. He describes no church service or formal religious observance.
 That gap separates the meal from the colonists' own idea of thanksgiving. For the Pilgrims, the word meant a solemn day given over to prayer. Feasting with guests and shooting practice did not fit it.
 The "first Thanksgiving" label was attached to the 1621 meal long after it took place. Later writers and illustrators turned the gathering into an origin story for the national holiday.
 Wampanoag history adds another layer to how the event is remembered. Since 1970, a National Day of Mourning has been held in Plymouth on Thanksgiving Day. Organizers use it to draw attention to the effects of English colonization on Native people.
 The gathering produced no fixed date, no proclamation and no repeated ritual. Its place in the holiday's story comes from Winslow's brief description and from the meaning later generations gave it.
 Colonial days of thanksgiving in New England 
 Illustration: Quartz
 In 17th-century New England, a day of thanksgiving was a religious observance proclaimed by colonial governors or church congregations in response to a specific event. These days were called one at a time, and none was tied to a fixed date on the calendar.
 The trigger was usually a good harvest or a military outcome that the colonists read as a sign of divine favor. A governor or congregation would announce the day, and the community set aside ordinary work to attend worship. Prayer, preaching and psalm singing in the meetinghouse formed the center of the observance, not a meal.
 New England colonists paired these occasions with their opposite, the day of fasting and humiliation. A fast day answered hardship, such as drought, disease or a failed crop. A thanksgiving day answered relief. Both were acts of public worship. Either could be called whenever events seemed to demand it.
 Plymouth Colony offers an early example. In 1623, a summer drought threatened the colony's crops, and the settlers held a day of humiliation and prayer. Rain followed, and the colony then appointed a day of thanksgiving. Edward Winslow described the episode in Good Newes from New England, published in 1624.
 Military events produced similar proclamations. In 1637, Massachusetts Bay held a day of thanksgiving following the Pequot War. That conflict pitted English colonists against the Pequot people of present-day Connecticut.
 The word "thanksgiving" therefore meant something narrower to these colonists than it does today. It named a solemn day of worship set aside by authority. A shared meal did not make a thanksgiving on its own.
 The practice spread across the region as more colonies formed. Over the following century, several New England governments came to proclaim a thanksgiving most autumns, after the harvest was in. Even then, officials chose the date each year, and the day could shift from one year to the next.
 This colonial custom was regional rather than national. Each colony made its own proclamations, and no authority set a common day for all of them. A single thanksgiving recommended across every colony came only during the American Revolution.
 The Continental Congress thanksgiving of 1777 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The Continental Congress recommended that all 13 states set aside Thursday, December 18, 1777, as a day of thanksgiving after the American victory at Saratoga. It is generally described as the first national thanksgiving observance in the U.S.
 The call was a one-time recommendation. Congress named a single date and did not create a recurring holiday.
 The victory behind it came in upstate New York. British General John Burgoyne surrendered his army to American forces under General Horatio Gates on October 17, 1777. The surrender ended a British campaign to split New England from the other colonies along the Hudson River.
 Congress was not meeting in Philadelphia at the time. British troops had occupied the city in September 1777, and the delegates had moved west to York, Pennsylvania. It was there, on November 1, 1777, that Congress adopted the thanksgiving resolution.
 Samuel Adams of Massachusetts served on the three-member committee that drafted the text, alongside Richard Henry Lee of Virginia and Daniel Roberdeau of Pennsylvania. The language was openly religious. It asked Americans to give thanks for the year's blessings, to confess their sins and to pray for the success of the war.
 Congress had no power to impose a holiday on the states. Its resolution recommended that the legislative or executive authorities of each state set the day apart. It also asked that servile labor, along with recreation unsuited to a solemn occasion, be put aside on that date.
 That limit reflected how the confederation worked. The Articles of Confederation, which Congress approved in November 1777, left most domestic authority with the states.
 The Continental Army marked the day while on the move. George Washington's troops observed it in camp at Gulph Mills, Pennsylvania, a day before marching into winter quarters at Valley Forge. Joseph Plumb Martin, a Connecticut private, later recalled in his memoir that the soldiers' holiday ration amounted to a little rice and a spoonful of vinegar.
 The 1777 resolution gave the country its first example of a national body calling for thanks after a specific public event. Congress went on to recommend other thanksgiving days during the Revolutionary War, each on a date of its own choosing.
 George Washington's 1789 Thanksgiving proclamation 
 Illustration: Quartz
 George Washington issued the first presidential Thanksgiving proclamation on October 3, 1789. It named Thursday, November 26, 1789, as a day of public thanksgiving and prayer across the new nation. He acted at the request of Congress, and the day applied to that year only.
 The request came from the first Congress under the Constitution, which met in New York City, then the national capital. In September 1789, Representative Elias Boudinot of New Jersey proposed a resolution asking the president to recommend such a day. The resolution tied the thanks to the opportunity Americans had been given to establish a constitutional government peaceably.
 Not every lawmaker supported the idea. Representative Aedanus Burke of South Carolina objected that it copied European practice. Representative Thomas Tucker, also of South Carolina, argued that a religious observance was a matter for the states rather than the federal government. The measure passed anyway, and Washington took up the request.
 The proclamation came early in the life of the federal government. Washington had been inaugurated on April 30, 1789, and Congress had first met that spring. The text asked Americans to give thanks for the peaceful and rational way their constitutional government had been formed. It also cited divine protection during the Revolutionary War. It closed by asking for prayers that the new government would be wise and just.
 The document was a recommendation, not a command. It set no penalty for ignoring it and created no legal holiday. It also did not establish a recurring date. Washington did not issue a proclamation the following year, and the 1789 observance did not become an annual custom.
 Washington returned to the idea once more. On January 1, 1795, he proclaimed a day of thanksgiving for February 19 of that year. That observance followed the suppression of the Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania. It fell in winter rather than late autumn.
 The 1789 proclamation was the first time a president under the Constitution called the whole country to give thanks on a single day. Presidents who later revived the practice used the same tool — a proclamation issued by the executive. That approach held for generations, until Congress wrote a fixed date into law.
 Why Jefferson refused Thanksgiving proclamations and Madison issued them 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Thomas Jefferson declined to issue national thanksgiving proclamations during his presidency, arguing that the Constitution kept the federal government out of religious matters. James Madison, his successor, took the opposite course and issued proclamations of prayer and thanksgiving, including during the War of 1812.
 Jefferson served two terms, from 1801 to 1809, without issuing one. He set out his reasoning in an 1808 letter to the Rev. Samuel Miller, a Presbyterian clergyman. Jefferson wrote that the Constitution barred the federal government from directing religious exercises. He also held that any authority over religion not given to the federal government remained with the states.
 In his view, a presidential recommendation was not harmless. Even framed as a suggestion rather than an order, it would carry the authority of the office behind it. Jefferson saw that as a step toward federal direction of worship.
 The position matched Jefferson's wider record on religion and government. He wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, which the state's legislature passed in 1786. His 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptist Association used the phrase "wall of separation between church and state."
 Madison had a long record of his own on religious liberty. He was a principal author of the Bill of Rights, including the First Amendment's religion clauses. He also steered Jefferson's religious freedom statute through the Virginia legislature. Yet as president he called on Americans to observe days of prayer and thanksgiving, tied to the War of 1812 with Britain. In private writings after leaving office, he questioned whether such proclamations were proper.
 The split between the third and fourth presidents shows how unsettled the practice was. No law required a national thanksgiving, and no date was fixed. Each president decided for himself whether to issue one.
 That pattern held for decades. Federal proclamations appeared in some years and not in others. Governors, particularly in New England, kept naming their own thanksgiving days, and those dates varied from state to state. A single national day observed every year did not yet exist.
 Sarah Josepha Hale's campaign for a national Thanksgiving 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Sarah Josepha Hale, the editor of Godey's Lady's Book, spent years pressing for Thanksgiving to become a single national holiday. Her campaign began in the 1840s and ran through editorials and letters to governors and presidents. It culminated in a letter to Abraham Lincoln in September 1863.
 The magazine gave her a platform. Godey's Lady's Book was written for women readers, and as its editor Hale controlled what it printed. She used its pages to make the case for a national Thanksgiving again and again, rather than in a single appeal.
 Before the Civil War, the U.S. had no fixed national date for Thanksgiving. A day of thanksgiving existed only when someone in authority proclaimed one. Governors set dates for their own states, and those dates did not always line up. Presidents issued national proclamations only occasionally. Hale wanted one shared day observed across the whole country.
 Letters formed the second half of her method. Hale wrote directly to state governors, asking them to observe a common date. She also wrote to sitting presidents, urging them to proclaim a national day. That approach went straight to the officials who could act on their own authority. A governor or a president could name a day of thanksgiving by proclamation, without waiting for a legislature to pass a law.
 The effort was long. It stretched across the 1840s, the 1850s and the early 1860s. Over that span, the White House changed hands several times. The sectional conflict that ended in civil war deepened in the same years. Hale kept writing through each change of administration.
 Her September 1863 letter went to Lincoln while the Civil War was still being fought. A few weeks later, on October 3, 1863, Lincoln issued a proclamation calling for a national day of thanksgiving. The proclamation named the last Thursday of November, giving the country the kind of shared date Hale had sought.
 Hale's name also survives in a different corner of American culture. She is credited with writing the poem "Mary Had a Little Lamb." Her Thanksgiving campaign is remembered instead for the shared national date it pursued.
 Lincoln's 1863 proclamation setting the last Thursday of November 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Abraham Lincoln issued a proclamation on October 3, 1863, calling on Americans to observe the last Thursday of November as a day of thanksgiving and praise. It is the first in the series of annual presidential Thanksgiving proclamations that has continued since.
 The proclamation came in the middle of the Civil War. It did not mark a single battlefield victory. Instead, it set the year's harvests and ordinary life against the backdrop of a war still being fought.
 Secretary of State William Seward is generally credited with drafting the proclamation. Lincoln issued it under his own name as president.
 The text addressed "my fellow citizens in every part of the United States." It extended the same invitation to "those who are at sea and those who are sojourning in foreign lands." It asked them to set apart the day "as a day of Thanksgiving and Praise to our beneficent Father who dwelleth in the Heavens."
 The proclamation also asked Americans to remember people left grieving by the conflict. It urged citizens to commend to divine care "all those who have become widows, orphans, mourners or sufferers in the lamentable civil strife." That passage tied the observance directly to the war's human cost.
 The October proclamation was not Lincoln's first wartime call for national thanks that year. In July 1863, after Union victories at Gettysburg and Vicksburg, he proclaimed a national thanksgiving. That observance answered specific military news. The October proclamation was broader in purpose.
 The proclamation's wording covered one year. It asked Americans to observe "the last Thursday of November next," which meant November 26, 1863. It did not set a standing date for later years. Even so, its choice of a weekday in late November gave later presidents a ready pattern to repeat.
 The proclamation arrived shortly after magazine editor Sarah Josepha Hale wrote to Lincoln in September 1863. Her letter urged him to make Thanksgiving a national day.
 The proclamation also had clear limits. It was a presidential call to observe a day, not a law passed by Congress. It created no legal holiday and bound no future president. Whether the last-Thursday date lasted depended on the men who held the office next.
 Yearly presidential proclamations and the 1870 federal employee holiday 
 Illustration: Quartz
 After Abraham Lincoln's 1863 proclamation, the presidents who followed him issued their own Thanksgiving proclamations every year. Repetition turned the last Thursday of November into the expected date, and in 1870 Congress made Thanksgiving a paid holiday for federal employees in Washington, D.C.
 Each of those proclamations was a separate act. No standing rule required a president to issue one. No proclamation bound a successor. The holiday continued because each president chose to renew it.
 Those choices kept landing on the same date. Year after year, the proclamations named the last Thursday of November.
 That date was still not fixed. It rested on custom rather than statute. A president could name a different Thursday, and no federal law would prevent it.
 The 1870 law gave Thanksgiving a footing in federal statute for the first time in one narrow area. It made the day a paid holiday for federal workers in Washington, D.C. For those employees, the paid day off was now a matter of law.
 Even that protection depended on the president. The law did not name a date. The paid holiday fell on whichever day the president proclaimed that year. Congress had attached a legal benefit to a choice it left in executive hands.
 The law had other limits. It covered federal employees in the District of Columbia, not the country at large. Workers elsewhere and in private jobs gained no federal right to the day off.
 The result was a gap between custom and law. Across the country, the last Thursday functioned as the expected date. The legal footing covered only one group of workers in one city. The date itself remained a presidential decision renewed each autumn.
 That gap mattered little as long as presidents kept to the familiar date. It would matter only if one of them broke the pattern.
 Franksgiving: Roosevelt moves Thanksgiving earlier in 1939 
 Illustration: Quartz
 In 1939, President Franklin D. Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving up one week, to Thursday, November 23. He acted after retailers asked for a longer holiday shopping season. The moved date became known as "Franksgiving."
 The calendar created the opening. November 1939 had five Thursdays, falling on the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th. Under the custom presidents had followed since Abraham Lincoln's 1863 proclamation, the holiday belonged on the last Thursday of the month. That would have put Thanksgiving on November 30, 25 days before Christmas.
 Roosevelt chose the fourth Thursday instead. In most years, the fourth Thursday and the last Thursday are the same day. November has 30 days, so a fifth Thursday appears only when the month begins on a Wednesday or a Thursday. November 1939 began on a Wednesday. That left a full week between the two possible dates.
 The request came while the U.S. economy was still recovering from the Great Depression. Moving the holiday earlier added a week to the stretch between Thanksgiving and Christmas. For stores, that meant seven more days of holiday sales.
 Roosevelt could make the change on his own because no federal law fixed the date. Thanksgiving still rested on a yearly presidential proclamation, the same tool Lincoln had used during the Civil War. Governors issued proclamations for their own states. Nothing required them to follow the president's choice.
 They did not all follow it. Some states adopted November 23, while others held to the traditional last Thursday. Accounts differ on exactly how the states divided. The outcome was one national holiday observed on two separate Thursdays, a week apart.
 The split had practical effects. Relatives living in different states could find their home states celebrating on different days. Offices, schools and businesses near state borders could face mismatched holiday calendars. The nickname Franksgiving linked the change to the president who had made it.
 The 1939 holiday did not settle the question. The disagreement over dates lasted until Congress wrote the day into federal law.
 The 1941 joint resolution fixing Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Thanksgiving became a legal federal holiday by statute when Franklin D. Roosevelt signed a joint resolution of Congress on December 26, 1941. The measure fixed the holiday on the fourth Thursday of November, where it has stayed ever since.
 Until then, no law set the date. Each year's Thanksgiving existed because the sitting president issued a proclamation naming it. The last Thursday of November had become the expected choice, but expectation bound no one. Roosevelt showed as much in 1939, when he moved the holiday a week earlier.
 The joint resolution took that discretion away. Congress wrote the date into federal law instead of leaving it to an annual announcement from the White House. By choosing the fourth Thursday rather than the last, lawmakers kept the earlier timing Roosevelt had pushed for.
 The two rules produce the same date in most years. They split only when November has five Thursdays. That happens when the month starts on a Wednesday or a Thursday. In those years the fourth Thursday lands on November 22 or 23, a full week before the last Thursday.
 Under the fourth-Thursday rule, Thanksgiving always falls between November 22 and November 28. The old last-Thursday custom could push it as late as November 30.
 Roosevelt signed the resolution less than three weeks after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, with the U.S. newly at war. Thanksgiving 1941 had already passed by then. The first holiday held under the new law came in 1942, when the fourth Thursday fell on November 26.
 The rule now sits in Title 5 of the U.S. Code, in the section that lists legal public holidays for federal employees. That section names Thanksgiving Day as the fourth Thursday in November. It sets the federal government's own calendar. States and private employers decide their own holiday schedules separately.
 Every earlier national thanksgiving, from the Continental Congress recommendation of 1777 onward, required someone in authority to call it. The 1941 law replaced that yearly decision with a fixed date.
